content_voiceover: This table, flagged as a must-know exam topic, contrasts the two classic patterns of therapy related AML. Alkylating agent or radiation related t-AML has a long latency period of five to seven years, often preceded by a myelodysplastic phase, and is characterized by loss of chromosome five or deletion five q, loss of chromosome seven or deletion seven q, and complex karyotype. TP53 mutations are common, the clinical course is insidious with cytopenias, and prognosis is generally poor. In contrast, topoisomerase two inhibitor related t-AML, caused by drugs like etoposide or anthracyclines, has a much shorter latency of only one to three years, usually presents as de novo AML without a preceding MDS phase, and is associated with balanced translocations such as KMT2A rearrangements at eleven q two three, RUNX1 dash RUNX1T1, or PML dash RARA. KMT2A rearrangements are the common molecular feature, onset is abrupt with leukocytosis, and prognosis is intermediate, depending on which translocation is present. This latency period and cytogenetic pattern distinction is a very frequently tested board concept.
keypoints: Alkylator or radiation t-AML: five to seven year latency, MDS phase, minus five/minus seven, complex karyotype, TP53 mutated, poor prognosis
Topoisomerase two inhibitor t-AML: one to three year latency, de novo, balanced translocations like KMT2A, RUNX1 dash RUNX1T1, PML dash RARA
KMT2A rearrangements common with topo II inhibitors; TP53 common with alkylators
Marked as a frequently tested exam topic
keypoint_voiceover: Two patterns of therapy related AML: alkylator or radiation exposure gives a long latency, an MDS phase, minus five or minus seven, and TP53 mutations with poor prognosis; topoisomerase two inhibitor exposure gives a short one to three year latency, de novo presentation, and balanced translocations like KMT2A, with intermediate prognosis.
